name: The Class for Representing a TV (Case 2)
description: Construct a class that represents a TV. The class should contain data that represents the TV's state (power on or off, current volume level). The state of the TV could be accessed or changed only through the getter and setter methods. The class should also include methods to change the state of the TV (turn on/off, change volume level). Assume that the volume level is an integer and ranges from 1 to 7 (both inclusive).

commentList: Purpose: def __init__(self): defines a special method that runs automatically when you create a new TV2 object, so you use it to set up the TV's initial state.
Syntax: def starts a function/method definition, __init__ is the special initialization name, (self) means the method receives the new object itself, and the trailing : begins the method body.
How it works: when you write tv = TV2(), Python calls this __init__ method for that new object so any attributes you create inside it (like self.__on) belong to that object.

Common mistakes: if you forget the self parameter you'll get a TypeError when creating objects; if you name the method something else it won't run automatically; wrong indentation or a missing : will cause a syntax error.
Misconceptions: __init__ is not a return value or a constructor in the low-level sense — it just initializes the object after it's created. You should not try to return the new object from __init__.

Best practices: use __init__ to set all needed attributes to sensible defaults (or accept parameters to customize them), keep complex logic out of it, and validate any inputs there so the object starts in a valid state.

commentList: Purpose: this line creates an attribute on the TV object that remembers whether the TV is on. By setting it to False you make the TV start in the off state.

Syntax breakdown: self refers to the current instance, __on is the attribute name, and = False assigns the boolean value False. The double underscore (__) is Python's way to mangle the name so it is treated as a private attribute.
How it contributes to the program: other methods (turn_on, turn_off, is_on) read or change this attribute so the object can enforce that volume changes happen only when the TV is on.

Common mistakes to watch for: if you forget to use self (writing __on = False) you create a local variable instead of an attribute and later accesses will raise an AttributeError. Also avoid using a string like 'False' or a different type — the code expects a Boolean.

Best practice tips: always initialize all instance attributes inside __init__ so every TV has a known state. Keep using the provided getter/setter methods (is_on, turn_on, turn_off) to access or change __on rather than reaching into the mangled attribute directly.

commentList: Purpose: You set the TV's power state to off by assigning False to the object's attribute self.__on. This line makes the TV report it is off so other methods (like volume_up or set_volume) will skip changing the volume when they check self.__on.

Syntax and semantics: You are assigning the boolean value False to an instance attribute named __on. The self. prefix makes this attribute belong to the specific TV object, not to a local variable. The double underscore triggers Python's name mangling (internally the attribute becomes something like _TV2__on) to discourage direct external access.

Potential errors and misconceptions: If you forget self and write __on = False, you will create a local variable and the object's power state will not change. Also remember Python booleans are True and False (capitalized). Note that double underscores do not make the attribute completely inaccessible — other code can still reach it via the mangled name — so this is a convention for stronger privacy, not absolute protection.

Best practices: You should change internal state only through methods like this so you keep control over valid transitions. Keep the attribute private and use clear method names (turn_off). If you need safer or more flexible access, consider using properties (with getters/setters) or a single underscore _on if name mangling is unnecessary for your design.

14.content: if self.__on and new_volume_level >= 1 and new_volume_level <= 7 :
commentList: You check whether the TV is currently on and whether the given new_volume_level falls inside the allowed range 1 to 7. If both parts are true, the following indented block will run and actually set the volume.

You use 'if' to start a conditional; 'self.__on' reads the private boolean attribute; 'and' requires both sides to be True; 'new_volume_level >= 1 and new_volume_level <= 7' checks the numeric bounds; the trailing ':' begins the code block you execute when the condition holds.

You should avoid common mistakes: do not use '=' (assignment) in an if — use comparisons as shown. Using 'or' here would be wrong because it would allow invalid volumes. Avoid using the bitwise '&' operator instead of 'and'.

You must be aware of type and evaluation pitfalls: if new_volume_level is not a number (for example a string) the comparisons can raise a TypeError. Because 'and' short-circuits you avoid evaluating the range checks when self.__on is False — putting self.__on first helps prevent such errors.

As a best practice, you can write the range check more concisely as '1 <= new_volume_level <= 7', and you should consider validating or converting the input (or raising ValueError) to give clear feedback when the value is invalid. Also use named constants like MIN_VOLUME and MAX_VOLUME so you only change limits in one place.

Decide how you want to handle invalid attempts: currently you silently ignore calls that happen when the TV is off or when the level is out of range; you might instead return False or raise an exception so that callers know the operation failed.

commentList: Purpose: you call tv2.turn_on() to change the internal power state of the tv2 object from off to on so that later calls (for example volume_up) that require the TV to be on will take effect.

Syntax and semantics: tv2.turn_on() is a method call on the instance named tv2. The parentheses () mean you are invoking the method; inside the method `self` refers to tv2 and the method sets the hidden attribute __on to True. The method does not return a value.

Common errors and misconceptions: if you forget the parentheses (writing tv2.turn_on) you only get a reference to the method instead of running it. If tv2 did not exist (you skipped tv2 = TV2()), you would get a NameError. Also avoid trying to change __on directly from outside the class — the double underscore triggers name-mangling and direct access is not intended.

How this affects later code: you must turn the TV on before calling volume-changing methods because those methods check the on state (they do nothing if the TV is off). By calling turn_on() here you ensure tv2.volume_up() can actually increase the volume.

Best practice: you should use the class's public methods (like turn_on) to change state rather than modifying attributes directly. Also make sure the instance exists before calling methods and include clear, descriptive method names so you (and others) understand what side effects to expect.

commentList: Purpose: This line prints a human-friendly message that shows the current volume level of the tv1 object so you can see the result of the previous operations on that TV.

Breakdown of syntax: print(...) calls the print function. Inside, you build one string by concatenating the literal "tv1's volume level is " with str(tv1.get_volume_level()). The call tv1.get_volume_level() returns an integer, str(...) converts that integer into text, and + joins the two text pieces into one final string to print.

Evaluation order and semantics: Python first calls tv1.get_volume_level() to get the numeric value, then str(...) converts that number to a string, and finally the + operator concatenates the strings. The printed value reflects the TV object's internal state accessed through its getter method.

Common errors and misconceptions: If you forget str(...) and write "..." + tv1.get_volume_level(), Python will raise a TypeError because you cannot concatenate a string and an integer. Also don’t drop the parentheses on get_volume_level — writing tv1.get_volume_level without () would give you the method object instead of its return value.

Encapsulation reminder: You must use the getter (get_volume_level()) rather than trying to access tv1.__volume_level directly. The double-underscore attribute is intended to be private and direct access will not work as you expect.

Best practices: Prefer clearer formatting such as an f-string (e.g. print(f"tv1's volume level is {tv1.get_volume_level()}")) or passing multiple arguments to print (print("tv1's volume level is", tv1.get_volume_level())) to avoid manual str() and +. Also consider whether you want to show the volume only when the TV is on (check tv1.is_on() first) for a more user-friendly message.

Syntax and behavior: print(...) calls Python's print function to write output. The string literal "tv2's volume level is " is joined to the result of str(tv2.get_volume_level()) using +. tv2.get_volume_level() calls the method and returns an integer; str(...) converts that integer into a string so the + operator can concatenate the pieces.

Possible errors and misconceptions: If you omit str(...) and try to use + to join a string and an integer, Python raises a TypeError. Also consider checking tv2.is_on() if you want to handle or warn when the TV is off.

distractors.description: You might pick this because you think the method can obtain the new volume in some other way (for example, by asking the user inside the method) so you don't need a parameter. If you use this line, calling tv1.set_volume(4) will raise a TypeError because the method only expects the instance (self) but you provided an extra argument. Even if you avoid the error by calling tv1.set_volume() with no argument, the method would have no direct access to the value you intended to set unless you add extra code to read it from input or a different place. This distractor is appealing if you confuse the purpose of setter parameters, but it prevents the intended external passing of the new volume value and breaks the test calls in the program.

Why you might pick this: you may think the only thing to check when changing volume is that the new value is inside the allowed range, so you leave out the power/state check. Step-by-step what this does: with this line, the method only checks the numeric bounds. If the TV is turned off, you can still call set_volume and it will change the stored volume. How this changes behavior: you would be able to change the TV's volume while it is off. That breaks the intended rule that the TV's state (on/off) must gate changes to the volume. Contrast with the intended check: this line omits any condition about whether the TV is on, so it does not prevent volume changes when off. This makes the program accept updates in situations where you should not be allowed to change the TV state.

You might choose this because you think the attribute is called volume_level (without the double underscores) or you don't understand how the double-underscore name makes the attribute private. If you use this line, Python will create or update a different, public attribute named volume_level, while the actual private attribute that the class methods and getters use remains unchanged. That means when you call the getter, you'll still get the old volume value — the change appears to do nothing from the outside. There is no runtime error, which makes this mistake especially misleading: your set_volume calls seem to run but have no effect on the TV's real state.
